opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way I approach it is to start from the inputs rather than from impressions of how capable the latest model seems. If you look at what's actually driven progress over the past decade or so, it's been a handful of fairly measurable things: the amount of compute going into training runs, which has been growing something like four to five times per year; algorithmic improvements that let you get more out of a given amount of compute; and the availability of data. Those trends have been surprisingly steady, so a natural first step is to ask how long they can continue and what happens to capabilities if they do.

Then you have to ask what the constraints are. Compute scaling eventually runs into things like chip fabrication capacity, power availability, the cost of building data centers, and how much capital people are willing to put in. Data could become a bottleneck, though I think synthetic data and multimodal sources probably push that further out than some people expect. So a lot of the work is trying to figure out which of these constraints binds first and when.

The harder part is mapping those inputs onto things we actually care about, like what fraction of economically valuable tasks AI can do. Benchmarks are useful but they saturate quickly and often don't track real-world usefulness very well. I tend to be somewhat skeptical of arguments that we're just a couple of years from full automation of most cognitive work. There's a recurring pattern where AI gets good at things we consider hard, like math competitions or coding puzzles, while still struggling with things that seem easy to us: long-horizon planning, reliable agency, operating in messy real-world environments. That's sort of Moravec's paradox showing up again. So I'd put meaningful probability on transformative AI arriving over the next couple of decades, but I think timelines are more spread out than the most aggressive forecasts suggest.

The last thing I'd add is that you have to think about feedback loops. If AI starts automating parts of AI research itself, or the economy more broadly, then growth could accelerate significantly. So forecasting isn't just extrapolating a straight line. You're trying to model a system where the outputs can feed back into the inputs, and that's where a lot of the real uncertainty lies.

r001.rationale: The response says forecasting is not just extrapolating a straight line, but does not clearly state that extrapolation itself works poorly.

r002.rationale: It says feedback from AI automating research or the economy could accelerate growth, but does not say this requires economic output to grow rapidly.

r003.rationale: It proposes examining measurable drivers and constraints shaping AI progress, including compute, algorithms, data, infrastructure, power, and investment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that forecasting AI is really hard, and I think people should be a lot more humble about it than they usually are. But that doesn't mean you can't say anything. The approach we take at Epoch is to try to anchor on quantities you can actually measure. So you look at things like how much compute is going into training runs, how fast that's been growing, how much algorithmic progress there's been, how quickly hardware is getting cheaper, and how much money is flowing into the field. Those are all things with a track record, and you can extrapolate them, at least for a few years.

The compute trend is probably the most informative one. Training compute for frontier models has been growing something like four or five times per year for over a decade now. That's an enormous rate of growth, and the interesting question is how long it can continue. There are constraints from power, from chip manufacturing capacity, from how much capital people are willing to spend. We've tried to model those bottlenecks, and my rough view is that the trend can probably continue to the end of this decade, but it gets harder and harder, and at some point you hit limits unless AI itself is generating enough economic value to justify spending hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars.

The harder part is translating inputs into capabilities. You can forecast compute pretty well, but what you actually care about is what the models can do, and that mapping is much less certain. Scaling laws give you some handle on it, in that loss goes down predictably with compute. But the relationship between loss and economically useful capabilities is murky. So there I think you have to be more uncertain, and I try to hold wide distributions.

The other thing I'd say is that I tend to be somewhat more skeptical of very short timelines than a lot of people in the field. Not because I think AI progress is slow, it's clearly very fast, but because I think people underestimate how many things have to go right for something like full automation of the economy. There's a long tail of tasks that involve agency, long horizons, interacting with the physical world, dealing with messy contexts. Current systems are impressive on benchmarks and much weaker on those things. So my median for transformative, economy-wide effects is probably later than, say, the people who think it's two or three years away. But I also put real probability on it, and I think that's a pretty unusual situation to be in historically.

r001.rationale: The response says measurable inputs can be extrapolated for a few years, while the input-to-capability mapping is uncertain. It does not state that extrapolation is generally ineffective for forecasting AI development.

r002.rationale: It says AI-generated economic value could justify very large spending, but does not say that this output must grow rapidly to sustain further AI development.

r003.rationale: It proposes grounding forecasts in forces shaping development, including compute growth, algorithmic progress, hardware costs, investment, and constraints such as power and chip capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate a few questions that often get bundled together. How much compute will people use to train models? How much more efficiently will algorithms use that compute? And how will those changes translate into capabilities that matter in the real world?

The first question is relatively concrete. You can think about investment, chip production, and power requirements. Algorithmic progress is harder to forecast, but you can still look at how much less compute it takes over time to achieve a given level of performance. The really difficult step is translating those trends into something like, “When will AI be able to do most of the work a human researcher does?” A benchmark score doesn’t directly answer that.

So I’d start with those measurable trends, but put a lot of uncertainty around the connection to economically useful capabilities. And I’d look at a range of scenarios rather than take one extrapolation too literally. In particular, if AI starts substantially accelerating AI research itself, then the process generating progress changes, and historical trends become a less reliable guide.

The goal, to me, is to have a forecast where you can explain what’s driving it and what evidence would make you change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against taking one extrapolation too literally and says historical trends may become less reliable if AI accelerates AI research, but it does not state that extrapolation generally works poorly for forecasting AI development.

r002.rationale: The response mentions economically useful capabilities and AI accelerating AI research, but does not say that a feedback loop from AI-generated economic output requires rapid growth in that output.

r003.rationale: It proposes considering forces shaping development, including investment, chip production, power requirements, algorithmic efficiency, and possible AI acceleration of AI research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to break the question down into things that we can forecast with somewhat different levels of confidence. One is how much compute people are going to use to train AI systems. Another is how efficiently they're going to use that compute. And then there's the question of what capabilities you get out of those inputs, which is considerably harder.

For compute, you can look at investment, chip production, improvements in hardware, and constraints like power and the time it takes to build data centers. Those give you some basis for extrapolation. For algorithmic progress, you can look at how the compute required to achieve a particular level of performance has changed over time, although there's a question about how representative any particular benchmark is.

The difficult step is translating those trends into something like, when will AI be able to do most of the work a human can do? We don't have a very good quantitative model of that. You can have fairly smooth improvements in training loss and still see changes in practical usefulness that are much less predictable.

So I would use these trends to constrain my expectations, but I wouldn't take a particular date too seriously. I'd want a range of scenarios, and I'd ask which uncertainties are actually driving the differences between them. Is it investment? Is it whether existing methods continue to improve? Is it whether systems can reliably carry out long tasks? That gives you a more useful forecast, because you can update it as you get evidence about those specific questions.

r001.rationale: The response says extrapolation can provide a basis for expectations, while noting limits and uncertainty. It does not state that extrapolation works poorly overall.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a feedback loop between AI-generated economic output and further AI development, or the need for rapid economic growth.

r003.rationale: It proposes examining drivers such as investment, chip production, hardware improvements, power, and data-center constraints, then updating forecasts based on which uncertainties drive outcomes.
